pll1d40c2-d1e3501.summary: Defines: predestination is the preparation of grace, divine election before the world; reprobation is foreknowledge of some people's iniquity and preparation of their damnation. Predestination's effect is grace that justifies, helps us live well and persevere, and beatifies; reprobation involves two things: iniquity, foreknown but not prepared, and eternal punishment, foreknown and prepared.
claims: Reprobation is foreknowledge of iniquity and preparation of damnation.
God foreknows but does not prepare iniquity; he prepares punishment.

pll1d40c2-d1e3518.summary: Cites Augustine to Prosper and Hilary: sinners are foreknown in their sins, not prepared for them; punishment is prepared.
claims: Sinners are foreknown, not prepared; punishment is prepared.

pll1d40c2-d1e3538.summary: Cites Augustine, De bono perseverantiae: God prepared in his foreknowledge his goods for whom he willed, and foreknew that he would give them to all to whom he gives them.
claims: God prepared his goods for those he willed.

pll1d40c2-d1e3559.summary: Cites Fulgentius: God prepared eternal fire for the wicked justly, to suffer punishment, but not to commit sins; he prepared what divine equity would repay, not what human iniquity would commit, and was never the preparer of wickedness.

pll1d40c2-d1e3574.summary: Concludes: predestination is foreknowledge and preparation of God's benefits by which those freed are surely freed; reprobation is foreknowledge of unending malice in some and preparation of unending punishment. As grace is the effect of predestination, hardening is in a way the effect of reprobation.
claims: Hardening is in a way the effect of reprobation.

pll1d40c2-d1e3577.summary: Cites Augustine to Sixtus: God hardens not by imparting malice but by not imparting grace, which they neither deserve nor merit; rather they deserve that it not be given.
claims: God hardens by withholding grace, not by imparting malice.

pll1d40c2-d1e3597.summary: Reads Rom 9:18 accordingly: mercy means predestination and its effect, the giving of grace; hardening means the withholding of grace.
claims: Mercy is the giving of grace; hardening is its withholding.

pll1d40c2-d1e3614.summary: Cites Augustine to Simplician: God does not harden by compelling sin but by not granting some sinners the mercy of justification, by a most hidden equity, far from human sense, which Paul does not explain but marvels at: 'O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God.'
claims: God does not compel anyone to sin.
The withholding of grace rests on a hidden equity.

pl-l1d40c2.summary: Defines reprobation as the counterpart of predestination. Predestination is the preparation of grace, divine election before the world, whose effect is grace that justifies and helps us persevere here and beatifies hereafter. Reprobation is foreknowledge of some people's iniquity and preparation of their damnation: God foreknows but does not prepare the iniquity, and foreknows and prepares the eternal punishment (Augustine, Fulgentius). The effect of reprobation is in a way hardening, which God effects not by imparting malice but by not imparting grace, which they do not deserve. 'He has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills' (Rom 9:18) refers to the giving and withholding of grace by a most hidden equity, before which Paul could only marvel (Rom 11:33).
claims: Predestination is the preparation of grace, with grace in this life and glory as its effects.
Reprobation is foreknowledge of unrepented iniquity and preparation of endless punishment.
God foreknows sin but does not prepare it; he prepares punishment.
God was never the preparer of wickedness.
Hardening means not giving grace, not imparting malice.
The withholding of grace rests on a hidden equity beyond human understanding.
